headline: Parliament Advances Conservation Overhaul as Abuse-in-Care Redress Bill Passes Second Reading
summary: Parliament advanced contested changes to conservation law and the structure of the environmental ministry, while passing an abuse-in-care redress bill’s second reading despite opposition from Labour, the Greens and Te Pāti Māori over its treatment of some survivors. Question time focused on power prices, youth employment and retirement-village repayments, and ministers defended fast-track approvals as a source of homes and jobs. The sitting also progressed overseas-adoption safeguards and Treaty settlements, and heard Judith Collins’ valedictory address; several proceedings continued into an extended sitting on Wednesday.

topicSummaries.topic: Greens Challenge Government on Power Prices and Gentailer Profits
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: Electricity costs affect household budgets and the ability of families to heat their homes.
topicSummaries.content: Green co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick pressed Prime Minister Christopher Luxon on whether government-majority-owned electricity companies should reduce prices and whether their profits were excessive, citing an increase in households unable to heat their homes adequately. Luxon said expanding electricity supply was the main route to lower prices and pointed to stronger Electricity Authority powers to enforce fair treatment of consumers. He did not directly quantify whether gentailer profits were excessive, and the exchange left open how quickly the Government’s supply strategy may ease bills.

keyExchanges.speaker: Chlöe Swarbrick (Green)
keyExchanges.quote: Will the Prime Minister’s Government use their majority shareholding in gentailers to rein in their profits and lower New Zealanders’ power bills?

keyExchanges.speaker: Christopher Luxon (National)
keyExchanges.quote: We expect the gentailers to be giving consumers a fair deal. That’s why we are strengthening the Electricity Authority with new powers to make sure that they can increase fines and make sure companies play by the rules.

topicSummaries.topic: Youth Unemployment Puts Welfare Policy Under Scrutiny
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: Young people’s access to work, training and education affects their incomes and longer-term prospects.
topicSummaries.content: Labour’s Willow-Jean Prime challenged Social Development Minister Louise Upston over young people not in employment, education or training, and the rise in youth jobseeker numbers since 2023. Upston acknowledged that young people are disproportionately affected by difficult economic conditions, while defending job coaching and the Government’s welfare reset; she said 84,000 people had left welfare for work in the past year. In a separate exchange, Rural Communities Minister Mark Patterson said funding for the Mayors’ Taskforce for Jobs had been reallocated rather than cut, after Labour raised a reduction in places in Kaikōura.

keyExchanges.speaker: Willow-Jean Prime (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: Is having nearly 100,000 young New Zealanders not in employment, education, or training a sign that young New Zealanders are on a better path?

keyExchanges.speaker: Louise Upston (National)
keyExchanges.quote: We accept that there may not be a job opportunity for all of them right now, but the work that we’re doing through that intensive case management, through job coaching, through the wide range of programmes that support young people, is to assist them to take up those opportunities when the job is there.

topicSummaries.topic: Retirement Village Repayment Proposal Sets 12-Month Deadline
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The timing of capital repayments can affect residents’ access to money tied up in their homes, including when they need funds for care or other expenses.
topicSummaries.content: Labour’s Ingrid Leary questioned Associate Housing Minister Tama Potaka over proposed retirement-village rules that would give operators up to 12 months to repay residents’ capital. Potaka said the proposal balances resident protections with the financial viability of the sector and would apply the new mandatory repayment rules to new residents rather than retrospectively to existing residents. He rejected a shorter three-month deadline, while saying other protections, including ending weekly fees when a resident moves out, would apply more broadly. The bill is expected to go through a future select committee process.

keyExchanges.speaker: Ingrid Leary (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: How is it acceptable to give retirement village operators 12 months to repay when it is the residents’ own money and, for many of them, time is not on their side?

keyExchanges.speaker: Tama Potaka (National)
keyExchanges.quote: We consider that we have struck the right balance between consumer protections and the need to have a viable, financially responsible retirement village sector.

topicSummaries.topic: Fast-Track Scheme Reports 21 Approvals and More Than 8,000 Homes
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The approvals are intended to support housing, infrastructure and employment, while the fast-track process remains contested over its effects on consent scrutiny.
topicSummaries.content: Infrastructure Minister Chris Bishop told the House that 21 projects had been approved through the fast-track scheme, including projects expected to provide more than 8,000 homes and generate investment and jobs. He cited three recent approvals: a Waikato housing and solar development and two Canterbury industrial developments, one expected to contribute more than $450 million to the economy. Bishop also said the Waihi gold-mining expansion could generate $5.2 billion in additional exports over 18 years. Labour MPs challenged the scheme’s benefits and raised concerns about its reception in Queenstown; the Minister argued that the pathway was speeding decisions and encouraging councils to improve their consenting processes.

keyExchanges.speaker: Chris Bishop (National)
keyExchanges.quote: Twenty-one projects have now been approved through fast track across New Zealand, with more to come.

keyExchanges.speaker: Rachel Brooking (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: They do not love it in Queenstown.

topicSummaries.topic: Conservation Bill Advances Amid Fears Over Land Disposal and Treaty Protections
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The bill could change how public conservation land is used, managed and funded, affecting access, biodiversity and iwi interests.
topicSummaries.content: The Conservation Amendment Bill passed its first reading by 68 votes to 54 and was referred to the Environment Committee. Conservation Minister Tama Potaka said the bill would streamline planning and concessions, allow targeted charges for international visitors at selected sites, and make some low-risk activities exempt or pre-approved. Labour, the Greens and Te Pāti Māori argued that the proposed changes would prioritise commercial use, lower safeguards around conservation-land disposal and weaken public and iwi oversight. The committee will consider the legislation and submissions before it returns to the House.

keyExchanges.speaker: Tama Potaka (National)
keyExchanges.quote: This bill enables the Government to introduce targeted access charges for international manuhiri at a small, selected number of visited sites.

keyExchanges.speaker: Priyanca Radhakrishnan (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: It allows the Minister to sell off 60 percent of conservation land.

topicSummaries.topic: Ministry for the Environment Merger Passes Second Reading
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The change would place environmental functions inside a larger ministry responsible for areas including housing, transport and local government.
topicSummaries.content: The Environment (Disestablishment of the Ministry for the Environment) Amendment Bill passed its second reading by 68 votes to 54. Environment Minister Nicola Grigg said the ministry’s statutory functions would continue within the proposed Ministry of Cities, Environment, Regions and Transport, with an annual report on those functions added to the bill. Labour and Green MPs argued that merging the ministry could reduce the visibility and independence of environmental advice, particularly on climate, water and biodiversity. Opponents also questioned the short select committee process; the next stage is consideration of the bill’s further passage through Parliament.

keyExchanges.speaker: Nicola Grigg (National)
keyExchanges.quote: In a phrase, this bill is about changing form, not function.

keyExchanges.speaker: Dan Rosewarne (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: A ministry can push back. A secretary answers directly to the Minister, who controls their appointment and their performance reviews and then their future roles

topicSummaries.topic: Government Plans to Bar Climate-Damage Tort Claims
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The proposed change could remove a route for people to seek compensation from companies for climate-related harm, while leaving existing emissions rules in place.
topicSummaries.content: Justice Minister Paul Goldsmith said the Government would amend the Climate Change Response Act to prevent courts from finding companies liable in tort for climate damage caused by greenhouse-gas emissions. He argued that climate policy should be set by Parliament and the executive, and that the change would provide businesses with certainty without altering emissions-trading obligations or national climate targets. Green co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick questioned who would bear the cost of harm if claims against private companies were barred. The announcement was made during question time; no bill stage or vote on the proposed amendment was recorded in the proceedings.

keyExchanges.speaker: Paul Goldsmith (National)
keyExchanges.quote: Therefore, the Government will amend the Climate Change Response Act 2002 to prevent findings of tort liability for activities that involve the emissions of greenhouse gas and climate change harm.

keyExchanges.speaker: Chlöe Swarbrick (Green)
keyExchanges.quote: If New Zealanders cannot seek compensation from private companies for the harms of their emissions, who pays?

topicSummaries.topic: Abuse-in-Care Redress Bill Passes Second Reading Despite Survivor Concerns
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The bill will shape financial and other redress for people harmed in State care, including survivors with serious violent or sexual convictions.
topicSummaries.content: The Redress System for Abuse in Care Bill passed its second reading by 68 votes to 54, after amendments recommended by the Social Services and Community Committee were agreed. The Government said an independent redress officer would assess financial claims from survivors sentenced to at least five years for specified serious violent or sexual offences; the Minister said fewer than 2 percent of checked survivors were in scope and they could still receive other forms of redress or seek to overturn the presumption. The bill also extends redress to abuse in State mental health facilities from July 1993 to June 2022 and adds provisions for terminally ill survivors and claims continued by families or estates. Labour, the Greens and Te Pāti Māori opposed the bill, saying the restrictions conflict with the Royal Commission’s recommendations and could further harm survivors; the Government argued the process protects the credibility of the scheme.

keyExchanges.speaker: Erica Stanford (National)
keyExchanges.quote: Of the survivors that have completed the declaration and the criminal record-checking process to date, less than 2 percent have been identified as being in the scope of the provision.

keyExchanges.speaker: Willow-Jean Prime (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: Labour remains clear about this bill. We oppose it. We appreciate the work that the Social Services and Community Committee has done to make some improvements to the bill, and the Lead Coordination Minister for the Government’s Response to the Royal Commission’s Report into Historical Abuse in State Care and in the Care of Faith-based Institutions for recent announcements which we support. But the fact remains that the bill is unwelcome and ill-conceived—92 percent of the submissions to the select committee were opposed to this bill.

topicSummaries.topic: Three Hauraki Settlement Bills Pass; Whanganui Settlement Advances
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The settlements record Crown breaches, provide financial and cultural redress, and return sites of significance, while setting out a basis for future iwi-Crown relationships.
topicSummaries.content: In the extended sitting that continued into Wednesday, the House passed the Ngāti Rāhiri Tumutumu, Ngāti Tara Tokanui and Ngāti Hei settlement bills at their third reading. Their financial redress totals $20 million: $5.5 million, $6 million and $8.5 million respectively, alongside cultural sites and other arrangements. The House also gave the Ngā Hapū o Te Iwi o Whanganui Claims Settlement Bill its first reading and referred it to the Māori Affairs Committee, with a report due by 17 September 2026. That settlement provides $30 million in financial and commercial redress, $15.5 million for cultural revitalisation and the return of 27 sites, including Moutoa Gardens Pākaitore. Speakers across parties acknowledged that the packages cannot fully compensate for land loss and other historical harms; Labour MP Willie Jackson also warned that support must continue after settlements are signed.

keyExchanges.speaker: Paul Goldsmith (National)
keyExchanges.quote: Of course, it goes without saying that no settlement can fully compensate for the loss and prejudice that the people of Ngā Hapū o Te Iwi o Whanganui suffered.

keyExchanges.speaker: Willie Jackson (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: Too often, settlements are made and then settlements are forgotten.

topicSummaries.topic: Overseas Adoption Safeguards Bill Receives First Reading
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The proposed safeguards aim to reduce the risk of abuse and exploitation for children adopted across borders while clarifying their immigration pathway.
topicSummaries.content: The Overseas Adoptions Legislation Bill passed its first reading and was referred to the Justice Committee, with a report due by 24 September 2026. Associate Justice Minister Nicole McKee said it would replace temporary restrictions introduced in 2025 with immigration routes subject to safety checks, create a pathway for adoptions from designated countries and allow limited Family Court applications where there is a sufficient connection to New Zealand. Labour and Green MPs supported the bill’s progress but called for careful scrutiny of its effects on customary and kinship adoptions, surrogacy, citizenship and children with disabilities. The House heard that existing legal gaps had left some children vulnerable to neglect, abuse and exploitation.

keyExchanges.speaker: Nicole McKee (National)
keyExchanges.quote: I welcome any suggestions of practical improvements that ensure that the law will work as it’s intended to, but one principle will not change: the safety of our children comes first.

keyExchanges.speaker: Willow-Jean Prime (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: We have to be able to strike the balance between protecting children through legal mechanisms in the law and our processes and practices, but also understanding and accommodating customary and kinship practices.

topicSummaries.topic: Judith Collins Delivers Valedictory After 24 Years in Parliament
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: Collins’ departure ends a long parliamentary career and creates a change in representation for Papakura.
topicSummaries.content: National MP Judith Collins delivered her valedictory address after the Speaker announced that her resignation from the Papakura seat would take effect at 11.59 p.m. on 14 May. Collins reflected on 24 years in Parliament, highlighted work including the Agent Orange inquiry and prison smoking restrictions, and thanked colleagues, staff, family and constituents. She said she would leave politics for an apolitical role as the incoming president of the Law Commission. The party leaders supported her decision to depart without a by-election, she said.

keyExchanges.speaker: Judith Collins (National)
keyExchanges.quote: I now leave politics behind and move into an apolitical world with gusto and even relish.

keyExchanges.speaker: Christopher Luxon (National)
keyExchanges.quote: I want to acknowledge her and her 24 years of service to this great country and this Parliament.

conclusion: The Government secured key votes on conservation, environmental administration and abuse-in-care redress, but opposition over environmental safeguards and the treatment of survivors remains unresolved.
